title: Protocols for electrophysiological recordings and electron microscopy at C. elegans neuromuscular junction
protocol: Pick one adult worm from the NGM plate.
Place the worm into a small container containing bath solution.
Use a tip-broken glass pipette to suck the worm into the pipette.
Gently blow out the worm to wash bacteria off its body.
Repeat washing 3–5 times.
Transfer the cleaned worm onto a Sylgard 184 coated circular coverslip.
Immerse the worm in a small drop of bath solution (∼20 μL).
Place the coverslip on a cell culture bottle filled with cold water to immobilize the worm.
Remove extra solution using a micropipette connected by thin tubing to an Eppendorf pipette tip.
Adjust the worm body to an arc shape using the same micropipette.
Touch the dorsal side of the worm gently and quickly with a tip-broken pipette containing glue.
Repeat touching the dorsal side at different spots to solidify the connection between the worm and the glue.
Add back a 15–20 μL bath solution onto the worm.
Use a pipette with a very sharp tip to cut the cuticle from a point behind the vulva to the bulb along the dorsal side.
Remove internal organs including intestine, gonads, and eggs using an extraction pipette controlled by mouth suction via thin tubing.
Glue down the ventral edge of the cuticle to expose the ventral nerve cord and body wall muscles while applying positive pressure to the glue tip.
Take the coverslip off the ice bottle and secure it into the inner well of the recording chamber with silicone grease.
Apply gentle pressure to the coverslip using the cap of a 15 mL centrifuge tube to ensure a good seal between the coverslip and chamber.
Add a 20 μL drop of collagenase (1 mg/mL in extracellular solution) to the worm on the coverslip for cell digestion.
Incubate with collagenase for 30 seconds at about 0.5 mg/mL concentration.
Keep the collagenase tube on ice during application and incubation.
Transfer the chamber to the inner holder of the moving stage.
Adjust the position for easy access by both stimulus and patch pipettes.
Wash several times with bath solution via the perfusion system.
Add 1.5–2 mL of bath solution into the chamber.
Leave a very small volume of bath solution under the worm before glue application.
Hold the cutting pipette between thumb and index finger firmly to avoid shaking.
Incise the cuticle carefully without causing damage to the cell.
Practice dissection techniques for several weeks or months until mastery is achieved.
Position the recording chamber on the moving stage.
Place the recording pipette on the proper position.
Place the stimulus pipette (or pressure-ejection pipette) on the proper position.
Patch the muscle using standard patch-clamping technique.
Press the patch pipette against the muscle cell at the mid-point.
Apply suction to form a high resistance seal (gigaohm seal).
Change the holding potential to −60 mV.
Apply brief mouth suction to rupture the patch, forming the whole-cell patch.
Observe miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) at −60 mV membrane potential.
Switch the membrane potential to 0 mV.
Record miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs).
Place a second pipette above the ventral nerve cord of the C. elegans for electrical stimulus-evoked EPSC recording.
Apply an 85 uA, 0.4 ms square pulse through the pipette to depolarize neurons and record evoked EPSCs.
Position a pipette containing 1 M sucrose solution at the end of the patched muscle cell.
Apply a 20 psi, 2 s pressure pulse using Picospritzer to estimate readily releasable pool size.
Mix drugs such as acetylcholine, GABA, and levamisole in bath solution.
Pressure-eject the mixed drug directly onto the muscle body using a pipette.
Place the pipette filled with drug at the end of the patched muscle cell.
Maintain pressure-ejection parameters at 12 Psi for 100 ms.
Ensure correct placement of the stimulus pipette (one muscle distance from recording pipette).
Record all types of synaptic currents from the same muscle.
Replace solution and wait for at least 1 minute before repeating drug application.
Analyze minis using an Igor macro called “Amperometric Spike Analysis”.
Set a proper threshold before running the macro.
Use a 4 pA minimum threshold for most cases.
Select and analyze mini events above the threshold.
Integrate the averaged mEPSC current in Igor to calculate charge transfer.
Place a small drop of ddH2O in the middle of the shallow side (100 μm) of the A-type specimen carrier for freezing.
Scoop up OP50 so that it hangs from the worm pick and can be easily dropped into water.
Spread OP50 mixture in carrier to completely cover the bottom without overfilling.
Pick 20–30 young adult worms and place them in A-type carrier.
Place B-type specimen carrier flat side down on top of A-type carrier to form a “sandwich.”
Insert sandwiched specimen carrier into holder and activate freezing function for high-pressure freezing.
Repeat process with second carrier from the same strain.
Remove HPM100 liquid nitrogen storage dewar containing carriers from freezing rounds.
Pour carriers into an open container full of liquid nitrogen.
Remove each carrier from holder while submerged in liquid nitrogen.
Place two frozen carriers into a single numbered cryotube filled with liquid nitrogen then cap the tube.
Place carriers in cryotubes quickly.
Submerge cryotube in liquid nitrogen immediately after placement.
Transfer two cryotubes with samples into the bottom slots of a cryocane.
Immerse cryocane containing samples in liquid nitrogen within a transfer dewar.
Store transfer dewar in a 4°C cold room overnight before substitution begins.
Fill AFS with liquid nitrogen before initiating preprogrammed substitution protocol.
Pause AFS to allow cooling down to −90°C before sample insertion.
Connect AFS ventilation tube to the fume hood during remaining substitution process.
Place disposable ring-insert tubes for each frozen strain into flow-through rings.
Cut a notch in one ring-insert tube to indicate starting position.
Insert samples sequentially into respective insert tubes in clockwise order.
Place the ring containing the solution ring-inserts into a universal chamber.
Cool an apparatus specified for use as an unloading station with liquid nitrogen.
Top off liquid nitrogen throughout the transfer of samples.
Measure 0.05 g tannic acid (TA).
Add the TA to a 50 mL conical tube.
Add 50 mL of acetone to the tube.
Invert the tube until the TA is dissolved.
Fill the universal chamber containing the ring with the tannic acid solution using a plastic pipette.
Distribute the solution evenly in the center of the ring.
Fill to approximately 50% of the insert tube height.
Place the universal chamber into the liquid nitrogen filled unloading station.
Remove the cryocane containing the first sample cryotube from the transfer dewar.
Place the cryocane in the unloading station so that cryotubes are submerged in liquid nitrogen.
Precool all forceps tips in the liquid nitrogen.
Remove the cryotube with the first strain and place the specimen carriers into the first notched insert tube of the universal chamber.
Keep the carriers submerged in liquid nitrogen throughout the process.
Repeat steps for each strain, placing carriers sequentially into each l insert tube clockwise.
Place the universal chamber into the AFS and cover it with a disposable lid.
Restart the substitution protocol and note the time started.
After 1 hour, check to ensure samples are submerged in the TA.
Evaporate residual TA and liquid nitrogen in a fume hood.
Check liquid nitrogen levels in the AFS before leaving and fill if necessary.
Precool a universal chamber filled with acetone and another for waste liquids in the AFS.
Cool acetone for osmium tetroxide (either −20°C or 4°C is acceptable).
Precool pipettes by holding them in the chamber and then pipetting cold acetone in and out of them.
Pipette waste out from the external region while pipetting fresh acetone into the center hole of the flow-through ring.
Rotate the ring with the waste pipette to distribute the solution.
Repeat this process 3 times until acetone covers approximately 60% of the inserts.
Perform two sequential washes over a 1-hour time period following steps a-d.
Prepare the OsO4 solution after the 1-hour wash period.
Set up conical tubes in a fume hood, one containing vegetable oil or Vitamin C and another with 5 mL cold acetone.
Set up a plastic bag for solid waste.
Clean the OsO4 ampoule with acetone.
Cover the ampoule with tissue or plastic breaker to break the top.
Discard empty ampoules into the waste tube if necessary.
Place the ampoule with OsO4 crystals into acetone and pipette until crystals dissolve.
Transfer OsO4 solution into a universal chamber.
Place OsO4 containing chamber into AFS to reach −90°C and cover.
Deactivate residual OsO4 solution with vegetable oil or ascorbic acid.
Transfer deactivated OsO4 solution into the waste conical tube for disposal.
Clean forceps with vegetable oil or ascorbic acid followed by acetone.
Exchange acetone for OsO4 two hours after the washing period began.
Cover samples with a disposable lid.
Discard liquid waste in vegetable oil or ascorbic acid and use one of the oils to deactivate any solid waste.
Place deactivated solid waste in the waste bag.
Wash universal chamber used for OsO4 first with vegetable oil or ascorbic acid and then acetone.
Leave samples in OsO4 for 39.5 hours as temperature is gradually raised from −90°C to 4°C.
Prepare an embedding resin according to directions, shake or rotate the bottle for approximately 30 minutes to mix.
Fill a universal chamber with cooled acetone and place it in the AFS 30 minutes prior to the first wash.
Wash samples twice with cooled acetone following the wash protocol listed above.
Wash samples a third time after 30 minutes.
Prepare 50% resin by filling a 50 mL conical tube with 10 mL cold acetone and adding 10 mL resin.
Fill a universal chamber with the mixture and store it at 4°C or in the AFS.
Do a fourth and final wash one hour after the third wash.
Exchange acetone for 50% resin.
One hour after the final acetone wash, remove the samples from the AFS to room temperature.
Exchange the acetone for the 1:1 acetone:resin mixture.
Let this sit for 4 h at room temperature.
Transfer samples to polypropylene capsules with 100% resin.
Number a polypropylene capsule disc for each strain.
Place a small drop of resin into the capsule.
Using a pair of forceps, stabilize the flow through ring and grasp the insert tube.
Remove the tube with your palm facing up and invert to transfer the carrier into the resin.
Ensure samples are fully submerged in the resin; add more resin if needed.
Leave samples in resin for 18 h or overnight in a 4°C refrigerator.
The morning that embedding begins, prepare slides and embedding dishes.
Prepare top slides for thin-embedding by laying out one slide per strain plus extras on paper towels.
Heavily coat one side of each slide with Teflon spray.
Let the coated side dry for 5–10 min.
Repeat coating process for 3–4 coats to completely cover one side in Teflon.
Cut thin strips of parafilm and make small stacks 3 strips deep, two stacks per strain.
Set out one 100 mm petri dish per strain.
Number the dishes.
Place two toothpicks parallel in the bottom of each dish.
Label a slide for each strain.
Place the labeled slide on top of the toothpicks.
Place two stacks of parafilm on either end of the slide to determine thickness of embedding resin.
Set up microscope with light source underneath and top light.
Place polypropylene capsule containing resin-infused samples into working petri dish.
Use fine syringe needles (30 gauge) to gently pick apart bacteria cryoprotectant to remove worms from bacteria.
Transfer separated worms to the resin, spacing them out so they can be individually cut out later with a razor blade.
Angle Teflon-coated slide slightly offset from bottom slide and cover.
Place petri dishes in 60°C incubator for 2 days.
Use remaining resin to fill block molds for mounting worms.
Cure the blocks in a 60°C incubator for 2 days.
Remove Teflon top slide from embedded samples.
Cut out a piece of resin containing the worm, leaving resin around it.
Roughen the mounting end of a flat side of a resin block with sandpaper.
Apply a small drop of super glue on the roughened surface.
Place the resin-encased worm onto the block with the worm facing down.
Orient the worm head toward the front of the block for ease of access during sectioning.
Hold the worm in place until it sticks to the super glue.
Cover the entire piece of resin containing the worm with super glue.
Allow the glue to dry overnight before preparing for sectioning.
Replace the trimming/sectioning knife holder stage with the chuck holder stage on the ultramicrotome.
Place the worm block into the chuck and firmly tighten, ensuring it is secure without cracking the block.
Tighten the chuck into the chuck holder securely.
Using a fresh razor blade at a ∼45° angle, trim excess resin from the block underneath the embedded worm with a downward motion.
Take care to avoid cutting too close to the worm to prevent damage.
Remove the chuck from the stage and place it into the specimen holder on the ultramicrotome.
Adjust the angle of the block so that the area of interest of the worm will be perpendicular to the sectioning knife.
Rotate the chuck to 90°.
Trim the bottom and top of the block with the edge of the trim tool.
Trim the face using the top of the trim tool.
Rotate the chuck back to 0°.
Return the angle of the chuck to 0°.
Move the stage to the angle that corresponds with the angle used to trim the bottom, top and face of the block.
Rotate the chuck 5° to the left.
Trim the left side of the block using the right edge of the trim tool.
Rotate the chuck 5° to the right.
Trim the right side of the block using the left edge of the trim tool.
Repeat these trim steps until the block is a trapezoid shape with the top and bottom flush with the worm.
Ensure the block width allows for ∼1½ - 2 worm diameters on either side of the sample.
Angle the block face perpendicular to the area of interest.
Trim away 250 μm from the tip of the nose in 1 μm steps to reach the ventral nerve cord anterior to the vulva.
Ensure the angle of the block face is exactly flush with the angle of the worm at the area of interest.
Continue trimming until the face of the block is shiny and reflective.
Replace the trim tool with the diamond sectioning knife.
Turn off the top light and use the reflection of the knife on the block face to align the knife to the exact angle of the block.
Use 0.3–0.5 μm steps to check the distance of the knife from the left and right sides of the block face, and the top then bottom.

Make small adjustments to the block angle to match top and bottom distances and change the angle of the knife to make left/right adjustments until it takes the same number of steps on both sides to reach the block face.
Monitor the reflection of the knife on the face of the block; when the reflection goes black, the knife is near the block face.

When the block and knife are perfectly aligned, step the block back slightly and set the automated cutting parameters on the ultramicrotome using the reflection on the bottom of the block as the starting point and on the top as the end point.
Orient the specimen arm so that the block is below the knife to start.
Turn the top light on again.
Slightly overfill the boat with ddH2O so that a dome of water is just above the boat and water covers the blade.
Allow the blade to soak up water for between 10–15 min.
When the blade is wet, adjust the water level until the surface is reflective and appears silver, level with the edge of the knife blade.
Raise the block slightly above the knife blade.
Start the automated movement of the ultramicrotome specimen arm.
If no ribbon forms, remove water from the boat and repeat alignment steps.
Stop the automated movement after ∼25–30 sections.
Gently move the ribbon of sections away from the blade using an eye lash brush.
Carefully collect the sections on a grid.
Repeat until the desired number of sections is collected.
Clean the diamond knife according to instructions.
Set up a staining pad with 1 drop of 2% uranyl acetate per grid and series of drops of CO2-free ddH2O for washing.
Place grids on the Uranyl Acetate for 4 min.
Move the grids through the series of washes using a perfect loop.
Use lens paper cut into triangles to wick away excess water or allow grids to dry before moving to the next staining.
Set up a petri dish containing KOH pellets to create a CO2-free chamber and place the staining pad on top.
Set up the staining pad with 1 drop of Lead Citrate.
Place each grid on Lead Citrate for 2 min.
Move the grids through a series of CO2-free ddH2O washes using a perfect loop.
Remove the grids and use lens paper cut into triangles to wick any excess water.
Allow the grids to dry before placing them in the grid storage box.
Acquire images using a JEOL JEM-1220 transmission electron microscope operated at 80 kV.
Collect images from the ventral nerve cord in the region anterior to the vulva.
Perform analysis using the NIH ImageJ software package.
Annotate regions of interest.
Measure areas or diameters based on pixels/nm of acquired images.
Identify cholinergic synapses based on their typical morphology.
Define a synapse as a series of sections containing a dense projection and two flanking sections without dense projections.
Identify synaptic vesicles as spherical, light gray structures with an average diameter of ∼30 nm.
Identify dense core vesicles as spherical, dark black structures with thick membranes and an average diameter of ∼60–70 nm.
Measure distances of docked synaptic vesicles to dense projections from the closest membrane edge of the vesicle to the closest edge of the DP.
Consider vesicles docked when their distance to the plasma membrane is 0 nm.
Statistically analyze raw data using Prism 9 software.
Use one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple comparisons test to determine statistical significance.
